doc.title: Ray Bryant interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

title: His latest tribute recording and putting his stamp on tunes
summary: He puts his own stamp on others' tunes; a C Jam Blues chord was a planned piano arrangement.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Glad to hear that. Let’s just talk a little bit about your most recent recording here. You picked out an impressive list of piano players to pay tribute to and interpret their music. And you know I remember early in the interview you were talking about some people commented on how they thought you played “After Hours” better than the original. And I have to say that that may be the case for a couple of tunes on this record also. That your version of them is really is quite outstanding.
That’s nice to hear, thank you.

I’m not sure I can put this into words, but when I listen to some of the differences from the original recordings and yours, you have a really unique way with the melody. And you seem to put in little pauses in certain places where the original artist may not have done it. Is that something that you think of or is that just my own—

Well I haven’t been too conscious of that, but I guess to even want to record a song I have to sort of like feel to a certain extent that even though I didn’t write this song, I have to sort of like take over a little bit, and think of it as being a part of my — how can I put this — I have to put my own personal stamp on it, even though it’s not my tune. But if it catches my ear and I think enough of it and I get to like it enough that I want to make a record of it, then it’s going to take on parts of my own personality. I guess this is unconscious.
I guess maybe what I’m hearing too is you choose to not sustain some notes in the melody where the original artist did, and it gives it a little bit more staccato effect or something.
Okay. I wanted to play one little section of C Jam Blues, and just ask you about something that happened at the end of one of the choruses here.

Now, what I wanted to ask you is when you got to bar 10 or whatever, and you kind of hung on that one chord there, whatever that chord was, was that something that was planned? And did the bass player know it was coming? Or was it just one of those kind of things that happened spontaneously?
No, that was planned. Because that’s an arrangement. Yeah, he knew it was coming.
That was basically my question, because I’m always fascinated by when things like that happen, was it something you had an opportunity to say okay when this part comes—

No he knew that was coming. See that’s like a piano arrangement. I try to play the piano like it’s a big band you know, and bring in different sections, brass and so forth. So more or less it’s played basically the same each time. But it’s a piano arrangement so he definitely knew that that was coming.
